speechtext: On the order for introduction of bills:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO BORSTAL SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-TRANSFERS OF OFFENDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a matter which is represented to me as being of some urgency has been brought to my attention by the attorney general of British Columbia. I have discussed it with the leaders of the opposition parties, and I understand they have taken it up with such of their members as might be interested. I believe it will prove to be non-controversial.
The province of British Columbia set up a Borstal system for taking care [DOT] of male prisoners between the ages of sixteen and twenty-three years, and in that connection came to this parliament in the session of 1947-1948 requesting us to incorporate in the Prisons and Reformatories Act a little code of three sections referring only to this Borstal system in British Columbia, and therefore without interest to any other province.
Section 147A, the first section of this code, provides for the imprisonment of these prisoners in the Borstal institution called New Haven. In all these cases in which the prisoners could get three months or more of imprisonment in the common jail, it is open to the courts in that province to impose a sentence of three months or more definite, and then an indeterminate sentence in addition to that of any period up to two years less one day.
By section 147B, the lieutenant governor may appoint a board of parole in order to grant parole to these prisoners, and by section 147C, the lieutenant governor may authorize the attorney general from time to time by warrant to direct the removal of these prisoners from this New Haven Borstal institution to Oakalla prison farm. In this last connection the relevant words of section 147C are:
. . . there to be detained for the unexpired portion of the term of imprisonment to which such person was originally sentenced . . .
In that province a case has arisen recently in which one of these prisoners, upon being

Questions
transferred to Oakalla prison farm after serving his definite period of time, applied to the courts for a writ of habeas corpus upon the ground that as soon as he had served the whole of -his definite term of imprisonment he could no longer be detained in any prison in British Columbia, except the New Haven prison, for the indeterminate portion of his sentence.
There is no desire that any legislation which might be passed here would apply to that particular litigation, and such legislation is subject to the general rule of the Interpretation Act that it does not apply to current litigation. But what the British Columbia authorities are afraid of is that if this precedent were followed in respect of all those who have been transferred to Oakalla prison from New Haven, it might result in a number of prisoners being set at liberty. We therefore ask for certain amendments, which will be in the printed bill, which I have arranged to have distributed. These three sections will make it clear beyond any doubt that the lieutenant governor in council in British Columbia shall have the powers which it was contemplated he should have when in 1947-48, at the request of the British Columbia government, and using the language suggested by it, we incorporated these three sections in our Prisons and Reformatories Act.

111. Departmental administration, $418,340.

When the
house adjourned last night I was prepared to be quite brief in the comment I wished to make on this item. Even though it is the beginning of a new day, my intentions are still the same. I hope I shall be so brief as to set an example for those who may follow me in this and in other matters.
I think my first words should be those of commendation, not only of the minister but of the excellent men he has in his department for the carrying out of a new forwardlooking policy in regard to the fishing

industry. I was glad to hear him say yesterday that he thought the solution of the troubles of the fishing industry did not lie in the principle of price support. I thoroughly agree with that. There are times, and we have just witnessed one of them, when price support serves a very useful purpose. I am sure our friends in the province of Newfoundland will be glad to learn of this price support policy in regard to the distribution of their salted fish.
The minister is perfectly correct when he says that the most important thing that can be done is to follow out general policies which will lead to the general health of the industry. By that I mean renewing old markets which perhaps have been temporarily lost, and developing new markets. I think the general policies of the government which have led, and we all hope will lead, to a continuation of the high economic level of this country will also be reflected in the fishing industry. The industry is perhaps affected as much as, if not more than, any others when we have what we have known in the past as depressions.
The fishermen whom I represent hope that the western farmers will continue to be able to sell their beef at the very high prices at which it is selling today, so that the fishermen will be able to find a ready market for their product, which is more healthful, and we think more nutritious, than theirs. It is a product which can be sold at a reasonable price by those in the industry, at a much lower price than people have to pay for beef. Therefore I hope that the price of beef will stay just where it is, so that the price of our fish will stay just where it is.
I do not wish to take up too much time, but I feel I should point out just how important this fishing industry is to the constituency of Queens-Shelburne. Figures I have here, taken from the Nova Scotia fisheries year book, show that in 1948 the landed value of fish in the small constituency of Queens-Shelburne, with a population of only 25,000, was $3,250,000, and in that respect it stood third. Of this amount there were lobsters to a value of $1,500,000 landed on our shore. In this respect my constituency took second place in Nova Scotia.
The hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth knows, of course, that his constituency took first place in the landed value of all types of fish and in the landed value of lobster. The constituencies of Halifax and Lunenburg are the other two major constituencies, Halifax taking second place and Lunenburg, the home of the famous Bluenose, taking fourth place. It will be of interest to hon. members to note that although it has the reputation of being
Supply-Fisheries
one of the greatest fishing counties-and there can be no doubt that it is a great fishing county-Lunenburg has had to take a back seat in comparison with the constituency I represent.
I believe it should be said that the large production of high quality fish in my constituency is possible because of the skill and industry of the thousands of fishermen who fish along that rocky and treacherous coast, where the storms become very severe and arise in a very short time. Approximately a thousand small motor boats are operating down there. The number is rapidly increasing, and has continued to increase since the war. Many war veterans, upon their return from overseas and with the assistance they received from provincial and federal governments, have gone into the fishing business themselves and have purchased very fine boats. The size of the boats is increasing and the engines with which they are equipped are becoming better all the time.
This increase of course results in a large concentration of boats in these small coves and harbours. I believe one of the greatest handicaps to the expansion of the industry in the past ten years has been the lack of proper breakwaters and wharves. The fishermen I represent are most grateful to the Department of Public Works for extending the breakwaters and wharves which are so necessary to the operation of the small-boat shipping industry. In the last three years the program has been extended rapidly, and I trust the Department of Public Works, in co-operation with the Department of Fisheries, will continue this work so that it may keep pace with the expansion of the small-boat fishing industry.
While I am on my feet I should like to thank the Department of Fisheries for their help in making it more apparent to the Department of Public Works and to treasury board that this expansion is necessary, and that the growth of the industry depends so much upon it.
As evidence of the high value fishermen place upon this public works aspect, it might be of interest to mention that when I was home at Easter I talked with a number of fishermen and others in the fish business. My chief topic of conversation, to begin with, was to ask their views about old age pensions, which subject was being discussed in committee. It is our hope that something will be done about this matter in the near future. Almost all of the people with whom I talked appeared to be more concerned with the funds provided to establish breakwaters and wharves so that they might be in a better position to look after their old age security

Supply-Fisheries
and that of their fathers and mothers who were not blessed with too great wealth. These people felt that we should not drain too much money from the taxpayers of this country for the provision of old age security when, with some little help by way of providing public works, they would be able to look after themselves. I believe this is an evidence of the fact that the people I represent are not leaners. As has been pointed out, they do not qualify for unemployment insurance. I do not think they want anything like that, but they do want a better chance to look after themselves.
It might be of interest to the committee-I am sure the Department of Fisheries is aware of it, but perhaps it should be emphasized- that our fishing industry down there is practically all of the small-boat variety. Ninety-seven per cent of the fish are landed from small boats. In contrast to this, about sixty or sixty-five per cent of the fish landed in the other two larger fishing constituencies to the east, those of Lunenburg and Halifax, is landed by larger boats. When I refer to the larger boats I include schooners, trawlers, draggers and that sort of craft.
lit is clear therefore that the fishing industry is divided into two sections, small-boat fishing and large-boat fishing. There is no question about the quality of fish landed by small boats. The price obtained by small-boat fishermen is usually a little higher. I know, for example, that several firms will deal only with small-boat landings, because the quality of the fish is that much higher. Its quality can be depended upon.
I would ask the department to keep firmly in mind the great importance of this industry in western Nova Scotia. Some observers detect a tendency to change to mass production methods, but I think we should keep this matter of quality in mind. It is important, and I think all those connected with the business realize that. This is one way in which our sales can be expanded-by making sure that the quality is kept high.
It may be of interest also to note that the decentralization of production by small-boat fishing makes an even distribution of employment along the coast. The degree of decentralization in the fish business is striking, where the small boats are used. For instance, in Lunenburg there are eighteen fish plants, whereas in Queens-Shelburne there are sixty-eight. I believe it is fair to say that almost every cove and every harbour has at least one fish dealer in it, which, of course, results in the young men growing up and staying in their own villages. Some years ago there was a great movement back to the

land. Down there we have a back-to-the-sea movement, and we believe it is most important.
I am informed there is one great weakness so far as quality is concerned. Many wholesalers buy fish by the freight carload because the rate by freight carload is cheaper. In many instances this results in wholesalers buying more fish than they can sell readily. This means that they must carry over that fish, with the result that the fish carried over cannot be of the same quality as if it were marketed immediately. I do not know how difficult this problem may be, but it seems to me the department might consider the possibility of encouraging the shipping of all fresh fish by express only. I do not know just how this could be done, but I certainly think consideration should be given to it.
That is about all I have to say at the moment. May I summarize by urging the department to realize the importance of small-boat fishing when formulating its policy, and urging it to continue its assistance in having recommendations from the Department of Public Works approved by treasury board, so that larger quantities of high-quality small-boat fish can be placed on the market. I urge them also to continue research and assistance toward improving methods of transportation so that the quality of the product that reaches the consumer will be improved. I urge also that everything be done to keep this industry decentralized so that the fishing villages will continue to flourish for many years as the true home of free enterprise.

Mr. Chairman, after the
speeches that have been made on this administration item it is not my intention to extend my remarks at all, but there are a few things I should like to say on the individual items. Last year the minister made an excellent statement with regard to the prospects of the fishing industry in Canada, and I was hoping this year he would extend his remarks and indicate whether the policies which he suggested before had worked out for the benefit of the fishing industry.
On several occasions when estimates have been before us I have indicated that I felt it was a mistake for the departments to ask for blank cheques. In this particular case there is a considerable amount being asked for in connection with which no information is provided. For instance, we are being asked to vote a total of $8,931,590, out of which $3,109,477, or practically thirty per cent, is accompanied by no information with the exception that reference is made to temporary assistance. When you consider the

casual assistance that is provided for, this amount is brought up to practically fifty per cent. The committee should be told something about it. This year we are told that there are 1,292 temporary employees besides the casuals and permanents, but there should be a breakdown to show how many are inspectors, how many are superintendents, and how many are day labourers. The minister has been engaged in big business, and I know he would not want his manager to come to him and say he wanted thirty-five per cent of the year's outlay for purposes about which he would tell him nothing.
I hope the minister will give the committee a further statement. Later on I shall have questions to ask, more particularly with regard to the establishment of fish meal plants in my own constituency, and in relation to draggers.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries):
speechtext: The total number of people employed by the department at the peak of the season is 3,391, some of whom may work only a week, some a month and some two months. The regular staff numbers 1,526. There is a great fluctuation in the number of persons employed.

That is part of the information I was looking for. There are 316 civil servants in the department, with an additional 1,892 temporaries. Then on top of that are the casuals, which brings the total to the figure the minister mentioned. We have never had any information about this large number of temporaries. When are they to be made permanent?

This is the department in connection with which hon. members from Newfoundland might be expected to speak in extenso, but I shall condense my remarks to a few observations.
I am glad to see that the minister has regained his optimism about the future of the fishing industry in Newfoundland, even if he has abandoned his attempt to revolutionize it overnight by changing it from a salt cod fishing industry to a fresh fish industry. There is room for both, and a proper balance should be struck. If this is done, a great future lies before the industry.
The minister seems to have the most highly trained staff of any department of government. When I looked at the list in the annual report of the fisheries research board I was amazed at the high quality of the technical and scientific staff engaged in the department. I am sure that the majority of the fishermen do not realize that there is such a highly qualified body of men behind them who are studying their problems and trying to help
Supply-Fisheries
them make a better living. Some of the men in that list have quite a reputation; I notice particularly Dr. Huntsman, who at one time was associated with the fishing industry in Newfoundland.
As this report was in our hands before the estimates of the department came up, we had an opportunity to see what had been done during the year. This is the very point I made in connection with the geological report in mines and resources. I found it most interesting reading. There is one item on page 48 of the report I should like to draw to the minister's attention and ask if it really means what it says. In connection with haddock, it states:
Measurements in 1949 at sea and on shore during four trips of commercial trawlers have shown numbers of haddock discarded at sea of 47, 32, 71 and 49 per cent of the total catch. Varying percentages of the haddock below 50 centimeters were discarded.
That seems to be a tremendous amount of fish to be lost. I believe that the minister shares the enthusiastic outlook of his staff as to the new vistas that have been opened up by the enlargement of Canadian fisheries with the annexation of Newfoundland. Newfoundland has a great variety of fish that still remain to be exploited. We not only have cod, but also lobster, salmon, trout, mackerel, herring, plaice, halibut, clams and scallops. Then there are various processes of preparation and preservation, such as salting, drying, freezing, canning and shipping in the live state. Then there is investigation of stocks on the Grand Banks and in the different waters around the island, the location of these stocks, the establishment of hatcheries, and many other possibilities.
I might say that in reading this report I was surprised to learn of the work that has been done by the scientific gentlemen to whom I have referred in the discovery of the location of fish. Let it be said again, as Bacon said hundreds of years ago, that the fisheries of Newfoundland are more valuable than the silver mines of Peru. If properly developed and protected they should be like the prairie soil, a source of great wealth for ever to the people of this country. The increasing world population, and the scarcity and high price of animal products, particularly in time of war, have compelled the nations of the world to look to the sea more than ever for their food.
I should like to see the fishing industry of Newfoundland, as the hon. member for Queens-Shelburne said about his province, maintained on a sound basis. From a social as well as from an economic point of view the methods of fishing in Newfoundland were

Supply-Fisheries
ideal. I do not wish to see the fishing industry become centralized and highly industrialized like the motor car industry, unless the fishermen are to be partners and shareholders in the enterprise. The principle of private ownership, which is a very important feature of the Newfoundland fishing industry, must be preserved, and, I suggest, improved and strengthened. In the past I had the honour to be closely associated with the co-operative movement which was introduced into Newfoundland in 1936 from Antigonish. I may say, especially in the sale of live lobsters to the United States, that the co-operative movement has been outstandingly successful.
The provincial government is so alert to the value of co-operation in regard to the fisheries that the new provincial minister of fisheries has also taken the title of minister of co-operatives. The set-up in Newfoundland therefore provides a field of endeavour for any economist associated with the fisheries research board of Canada, and I hope there is one who is familiar with cooperative methods. Probably there are many, although I am not aware of it. I trust there is one who is interested in and conversant with the co-operative methods developed at Antigonish.
I cannot emphasize too strongly the necessity of building on the traditional methods of independence amongst the fishermen. I know that many of them are sometimes badly off at the end of a voyage when the fish fail them; nevertheless the principle is sound, and remedies can be found to cure the scarcity of fish. I am going to speak about one now. In my opinion the study and application of co-operative practices is the best way of improving the economic position of the fishermen.
I am forced to speak about an important need in many parts of Newfoundland, the supply of fresh bait daily. The Minister of Fisheries is familiar with the pressing need. The supply of fresh bait daily to fishermen who are using trawls or the hook and line is an absolute necessity. It is impossible for them to carry on without it. I wonder if the establishment of a floating bait freezer is not the solution for a large section of the coast. I am glad to see that the minister is making an experiment in thait direction this year, and I trust it will be very successful. I hope it will be able to operate in my district, because the constituency of St. John's West, although it is so largely concerned with the city, is probably the most important fishing section of the country. Five big trawlers operate a shuttle service
[Mr. Browne (St. John's West).!
to the Grand Banks from the south side of the city of St. John's and bring in large amounts of fresh fish.
From the south side of St. John's for 100 miles down -the coast to the Ferryland district, fifty miles up into St. Mary's bay, down to Placentia bay and another 150 miles up Placentia bay, in every settlement along that 300 miles stretch of coast there are fishermen who go out in boats, punts, dories or jackboats, to fish with hook and line, trawl, net or seine. A ready supply of fresh bait is essential to most of them if they are to catch fish. To have such a supply near at hand is also important, because it means that they can keep down the cost of catching fish, which will mean that there will be more profit. I feel sure that the minister is sympathetic to their position; because I have already drawn to his attention the need of places like Renews bay-where there is an industrious group of fishermen who sail out in jackboats many miles away-and Bay Bulls. I understand it was decided that there would be a bait depot at Placentia. I trust that the minister is still considering these matters and that he will not disappoint people who are expecting to have these facilities.
There is one other matter to which I should like to refer, the salmon fishing industry in the inland waters so far as the tourist trade is concerned. The preservation of salmon stocks requires a study of inland waters and therefore close integration between forest research and water supply. The maintenance of levels in lakes and rivers is a very big problem, and can only be done by co-operation between experts in the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Resources and Development. I am aware that at the northeast section of Trepassey river tagging was carried on for a short period, and the warden of that river also made some examination of all fish caught by measuring the length and taking samples of the scales to be sent to the biological station in St. John's. I trust that practice can be carried on in as many rivers as possible.
I noticed that there was tagging being carried on in Cape Royal river, which I know very well. It is a tiny river, and I do not think it is suitable for that purpose. The Trepassey is a very much better river. I have been going there for sixteen years, and I know it has a steady supply of fish except for last summer which was most extraordinary. For the first time the fish were prevented for weeks from entering the river. When the water level becomes too low in the river, fishing is finished. We have to try to keep people from cutting timber along the

banks of the rivers and lakes so that there can be a more even flow of water. If that effort is successful, then salmon fishing in the rivers will be, as it should be, a great attraction for tourists and will provide much pleasure for them.
That is. all I wish to say, Mr. Chairman, but I trust that the minister will give some consideration to the points I have raised.

Item agreed to.
112. Fisheries inspection, including fishery officers and guardians, fisheries patrol and protection services, $3,771,000.

I notice that there is an increase of $546,000 over last year. No doubt it is due to the number of extra employees who have been taken on. I see that there are 275 inspectors and other types of officers. I should like to know how many of these are inspectors or fish wardens in Prince Edward Island. If the minister could also give an idea of the work these officers are doing in Prince Edward Island, I would appreciate it.

Mr. Chairman, item 112 covers additional positions. Will the minister state whether the inspectors that were taken on from the Newfoundland service are on full time?
The staff of the Newfoundland board has simply been transferred to our department, and is on full time.
Does this also take in the wardens on the rivers?
I believe they have been taken over as well. We have recently taken over the inland fisheries.
And it applies to them? They will be permanent too?
I think they are, but I would not like to make the categorical statement that all of them are.

The minister does not know
how many of those wardens there are?

In connection with the educational program, I should like to know who is the fishing demonstrator, and lecturer, and what area he or she covers. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr, Chairman, I am making my annual speech on the small dam in my riding which has not yet been built. Before I do so I want to speak first as a representative of a fishing riding, to say once again how pleased we are with the steady progress which has been made in the development of the fisheries department since the end of the war. I have in my riding both the fish packing industry, and a great number of fishermen. Both the industry and the fishermen are pleased with the steady expansion of the service, and the conservation work which has been done. That does not blind me to the fact that there is still a cinder in the eye so far as my riding is concerned, and that is the little fishing dam on Sakinaw lake near Pender harbour, which is the chief fishing town in my riding.
I have talked about this for ten years. When the present Minister of Fisheries became minister he saw the need for the dam, and an item of $5,000 was put in the estimates. It is about twice what the dam should cost, but that shows you how small a problem it is. The fishermen tell me that when the previous dam was in place the sockeye salmon were there to the extent of about 20,000, which means a fishery of about $40,000 a year. It made excellent fishing for the old men and the boys in the area, because the fishermen themselves go far afield. I am much interested in this community, because I think it is typical of the very best fishing communities. The fishermen are mostly of Scotch descent. They do not ask for price support; they do not ask for big expenditures for fishermen's harbours; they do not ask for assistance in the construction of boats; they do not ask for free bait; all they want to do is to fish. They want to fish the year round, and sometimes they fish more enthusiastically than the department sees fit, and they have trouble because they are working too hard. The one thing they do want to make sure of is that there shall be fish there for fishing.
It is now two or three years since the item for this small dam was voted, but there have been continual delays in the building of this little dam. It could be built in a week. The latest delay is said to be caused by the Indians who own the land through which this stream passes. They are demanding a rental of $150 a year. The fishermen's union and I have taken it up with the local Indian band, and they have consented to reduce the rental to $75 a year. The local chief said that if a white man owned this land the government could not build on it without paying a rental, and after all, the
[Mr. Mayhew.l
Indians have as much right to their land as the white man. I must confess I am inclined to agree with the Indians.
Under this item I do not think it unreasonable for the department to do two things. First of all they should pay the Indians what they would pay a white man if he owned this property; second, investing a small amount of money to produce fish that can be sold is better than paying price support for fish that cannot be sold. I should like to ask the minister what progress is being made in the negotiations with this Indian band.

The member for Coast-
Capilano said the Indians had agreed to a rental of $75 instead of $150 for the land. This is the first time I have heard of that. They have been asking $150. It is true that $150 is not in itself enough to delay this or any other project, but it establishes a precedent or basis of calculation that would make some of the other projects we have in mind away out of reach. The department at the present time are proposing to build a fishway at Morristown, and that fishway will cost in the neighbourhood of $60,000. It also is on an Indian reserve. If we had to pay $150 a year for the privilege of having a few square feet to anchor the dam on each side of the small Sakinaw creek, then I do not know what we would have to pay for similar privileges at Morristown. So it is not just the $150.
I know there has been delay, and no one's face is redder than mine about it. First, there seem to be about as many steps to take in getting through a small project as there are in getting through a large project. Here it was to dam this creek. There were nineteen people that we had to get permission from. Of those nineteen people I think only one or two were residing there; the others were scattered around with domiciles in different parts of Canada. They had to be hunted up and their permission had to be obtained to raise the water level. That has been done. Then when we went to the Indian band, they wanted $150 as a yearly rental. The last communication we had on it was just a few days ago. The present minister in charge of Indian affairs has been most co-operative and helpful, and I think the matter will be settled soon. I do not think the hon. member will have to bring the matter up next year. I hope, however, that will not prevent him from making a contribution to these discussions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I will certainly ask the minister about it next year, and in view of what he has said, I hope that the answer will be that the dam is built.

May I ask the minister how many hatcheries there are, where they are

located, and what type of fish they are taking care of in those hatcheries? Is any special provision being made for Atlantic salmon? If so, where are those hatcheries? What investigation has been carried on at the Grand Banks?

We are not carrying on any extensive investigations at the Grand Banks; but so far as salmon is concerned, we are doing a great deal, not in one province but in all provinces. I think hon. members will recall that some time ago I said I thought that our efforts should be weighted towards the species of fish for which we could get a ready sale. One of those species is of course salmon, both on the Atlantic and on the Pacific coast. Although our Atlantic friends think we have not the right to call our Pacific coast fish salmon, nevertheless that is what we call them.
We are spending a great deal of money in clearing streams, in providing dams and in seeing that the fish get to the spawning grounds. We are fighting a hard battle not only to maintain our present supply of fish but to increase it. That battle is against industries that sometimes regard our rivers more as a sewerage system than anything else. We have to try to get fish up there and to get them to live in that kind of environment.
We are trying to protect the species against improved methods of catching fish. The kill of salmon from a commercial standpoint and the_ kill of salmon by sportsmen is increasing rapidly. I make no apology for having some increase in this item, and I think that the amount will probably have to be increased rather than maintained at the present level if we are going to win in this fight. It is not only for the salmon, but it is for the many other species of fish for which there is an easy market and of which we cannot find enough to supply the present market, such as lobsters, oysters, shrimp, and some ground-fish. There is a ready market for them. We are spending a great deal of money. We are not detracting or taking away from our efforts with regard to the others, but we are adding to our efforts in connection with those particular species.
The hon. member asked how many hatcheries we have. The number in Nova Scotia is 15; in New Brunswick, 7; in Prince Edward Island, 3. That makes a total of 25.
Is it proposed to establish any hatcheries in the newest province?

We shall have to give that matter consideration. We have only taken over for a few hours, as it were.
55946-275J
Supply-Fisheries
I am not making any complaint.

We have no objection to your bringing these matters up for discussion and pressing for them. We realize that in some of the provinces the fisheries are the basis of their economic stability. We are trying to work out plans with the provincial government, with the industry and among ourselves, so that all three will combine in an effort to maintain that stability. It affects particularly the province of Newfoundland, but it also affects New Brunswick, in a lesser degree Nova Scotia, and in a still lesser degree Prince Edward Island, which is so highly developed as an agricultural centre. It is a beautiful place, and we are not neglecting it. You have some districts in Prince Edward Island that we think are marginal, and we should like to do something about it just as soon as we can get around to it.

Last year I made a suggestion to the minister in connection with the conservation of salmon. I would appreciate some comment from him if he feels like making it. At that time I suggested that the only salmon fishing I know of is that which is done in Newfoundland, and at the mouths of the rivers; a number of the fishermen live there and they fish right at the mouth of the river. I made the suggestion that it might be well to subsidize these fishermen not to fish for a period of two or three years. It might be much cheaper than having hatcheries in Newfoundland. I think it could be easily arranged. I know the minister is aware of the situation, since he was in Newfoundland last year. The fishermen use nets close to the mouths of the rivers. They use cod nets. They cannot be prohibited. Because of the use of cod nets, the smallest type of salmon are being caught and the rivers are definitely becoming depleted. I should like to have the minister's comment as to whether he agrees with that suggestion or not. To me it appears to be a sensible way of handling this conservation problem. Nobody would be hurt, and the department would still be saving money.

It sounds like a simple way; but I think that if the hon. member were sitting in my position as Minister of Fisheries he would have to get larger premises to accommodate the delegations of sports fishermen who would descend upon him if they were robbed of their rights to catch some fish.
I did not say to rob them; I meant to pay them.

Even to delay them. With most of the fishermen there is no tomorrow.

Supply-Fisheries
That is our principal trouble, that there is no tomorrow so far as the fishermen are concerned. We are trying to create a tomorrow by doing a good job.

I merely want subsidies and support, not for the sport fishermen, but for the sea fishermen at the mouths of the rivers; pay them what their average catch would be. The result would be a great saving of fish.
And it would cost the government about $50 million a year.
Oh, not at all-not anything like that.
If you did it there you would have to do it at other places.
I merely suggest trying it as an experiment at a couple of rivers.

I was very much interested in the statement made by the minister. He suggested that fish for which markets are readily to be found were receiving consideration so far as protection is concerned. Mention was made of lobsters. My^ mind goes back to several articles that I read' recently in magazines published in the state of Maine, indicating that lobster hatcheries in the state of Maine are making a very favourable report this year. I have seen several statements of the kind. To my knowledge the hatcheries that we have in New Brunswick have nothing to do with lobsters.
As any member of the department who has visited the maritimes would know, there is no shortage of spawn lobsters in that territory. At different seasons of the year thousands and thousands of female lobsters, spawn lobsters, can be obtained. In the exchange of information between the minister's department and the United States department, is the minister in a position to say whether the statement I have made is correct? Has the fisheries department in mind at any time the idea of establishing hatcheries somewhere in the maritime provinces?
I might also mention that in my riding- and one's own riding is the one that one usually thinks of first-there is a lobster pound that was formerly used by R. J. Conley Company. It would be available at the present time for that type of work. I am sure it could be obtained at reasonable rental by the department, and lobsters are available at all seasons of the year in that region. I should like the minister to comment on that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
In reply to the hon.
member for Charlotte I may say that in the state of Maine the value of artificial hatching of lobsters has become so doubtful that the authorities there have cancelled plans for the

expansion of the facilities. Instead they are carrying out an extensive investigation to determine what happens to the small lobsters when they are planted. They are using the entire output of their rearing station for this purpose. Canadian scientists are keeping closely in touch with this investigation. It would obviously be unwise to undertake any program of establishing lobster rearing stations until further results of this investigation are available.
The parliamentary assistant has mentioned the value of lobster hatcheries. Can he give me some idea of the value of trout hatcheries in New Brunswick to the industry and to the general public?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: The great value of trout or salmon hatcheries is chiefly to restock areas where the species have become badly depleted.

I believe the same number of men who are employed in the trout hatcheries in New Brunswick could be employed in the rearing of lobsters. If that were done we would find in a very short time that in dollars and cents it would be worth a great deal more to New Brunswick than the set-up you have at the present time.

May I say a word or two in support of the minister's policy of increasing hatcheries and increasing the supply of fish throughout the country? I believe it is a fundamental principle that has to be recognized, and it is beginning to be recognized by everyone in Canada that we should do everything possible to build up our stocks of fish to their former abundance. I therefore support the minister in the expenditures that he now asks for, and I would support him if they were greater than the ones he now proposes.
I should like to bring one matter to the minister's attention. I am not quite sure whether he has to do with the fish hatcheries in parks. In my riding we have a park, and I suppose you will find parks in a great many other ridings, in which there are lakes and streams in which it is desirable to replenish the fish. There is a hatchery there, but up to the present time the reports that I have indicate that the hatchery, after producing the small fish, the fry, turns the fry loose into the lakes-
Is this a national park?

Yes, Waterton national
park in southern Alberta.
That is under a different department.

The principle is all right, anyway. The point is that the fish are turned into the lakes while they are tiny little

things. There they readily become the prey of oiher fish. It seems desirable, in fact it must be desirable, to have little pounds made where the water will be warm enough and where these little fish can attain sufficient size to be able to take care of themselves. I understand they would then be called finger-lings. I wonder whether the minister has taken steps to provide for little pounds in which the fish could grow up. I would support such a proposal because the wastage of little fry when they are put into the lakes to look after themselves is terrific.

National parks are not under the Department of Fisheries; neither are the hatcheries in these parks. This matter should be referred to my colleague the Minister of Resources and Development, who is in charge of tourist trade.

Is there any provision for correlation between the efforts of the Minister of Fisheries and the efforts of the minister in charge of parks? It would seem to me to be an excellent opportunity for correlation.

In addition to that, we do not administer fisheries in the central provinces. These parks are mostly in the central provinces; therefore the co-operation would come through the provincial government rather than through the federal government. We are glad to give any assistance we can when we are asked, but we have not been asked.

Do the minister and his department agree with the principle stated by the hon. member for Lethbridge, that instead of stocking streams and lakes with fry, have rearing ponds of various descriptions to raise them to the point where they are able to take care of themselves? I understand that in the stocking of fry the mortality is up to ninety per cent.
Our policy is to have hatcheries and to have rearing ponds. From the rearing ponds they go to the streams in which they are planted.
Under this item of fish culture I notice there is $112,899 for materials; and for the acquisition or construction of buildings there is an amount of $166,030. Where were the buildings purchased?

purchase of fish, eggs of parent salmon, water fertilizer, material for poisoning lakes, rifles, shot guns, ammunition for predator control, and screen clearance.

speechtext: There is one large item for the construction of the Morristown fishway for $60,000.
As the great lakes fishing industry is an important part of the industry in Canada, will the minister outline what work has been done in fish culture on the great lakes?
That is done by the province of Ontario. They administer their own fisheries and look after their own fish culture. However, we are willing to co-operate with them and to advise, if necessary.

Does not the federal
government make a contribution toward hatcheries on the great lakes?
I am told we do not.

On a question of privilege, I am wondering whether this protest movement in action to my left would come under your scope, Mr. Chairman. I note that standing order 12 says that Mr. Speaker shall preserve order and decorum. Could we have a ruling, or does it come within your authority?
There is very little evidence left of any breach of order and decorum. The sandwiches have been eaten.

What knowledge has the
department in connection with the successful canning of live lobsters?

This experiment was begun about a year or two ago, and we have not heard anything about it recently. We have very little knowledge of it. It appears to be an expensive process.

S upply-Fis heries
Is it successful?
It is successful in that the lobsters can be moved from one point to another and kept alive for some considerable time. But the expense involved is considerable.

Mr. Chairman, I have been in communication with the department for some time about repairs to dams on the Medway river in Queens county. Medway has been, and I think still is, one of the world's finest salmon rivers. The water levels have continued to drop, and it is felt down there that by erecting dams to hold back the water it would improve angling and help the situation considerably. Has any action been taken?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
The work being carried out on the Medway consists of the building of two small dams, one at Hog Lake and one at Black Rattle, with the main purpose of holding back the water for a longer period and thus enhancing the angling development during the low-water period of summer. The amount for the Hog Lake dam is set at $4,000, and at Black Rattle, $2,000. The Medway system at present is relatively clear. The main trouble was at Charleston, and it is now being removed. A fishway has been installed at Brookfield, and one at Harmony Mills.	Negotiations are now under way
regarding the screening of the intake of the power station to protect the downstream migrants in this place.

Item agreed to.
115. Oyster and clam culture, $78,900.

I notice there is an increase of $5,200. Is this because of taking in clam culture with oyster culture? What is the revenue from oysters in the maritime provinces? I understand that something over $300,000 worth of oysters were shipped from the leased beds of Prince Edward Island. What would be the royalties on those, and how are they collected?
Where is the clam culture taking place? What kind of clams are being cultivated? Is there any culture of quahogs? Some people are keenly interested in the quahog industry.

As has been pointed out, the increase here is $5,200. This consists of increases in permanent salaries amounting to $660, temporary assistance, $1,360; wages, $1,735; acquisition of equipment, $4,500. This makes a total of $8,255. Then there are some decreases in printing and stationery, and office equipment, $75; travelling expenses, $1,990; material and supplies, $950, and sundries, $40, making a total decrease of $3,055, or a net increase of $5,220.
What royalties were received last year? Where does the clam culture take place?
The over-all oyster royalties amount to $5,132.62. There is no specific area in which clam culture is taking place. It is linked in with oyster culture.

What progress has been made in the protection of oyster beds in Cumberland county? The department had undertaken certain work near Wallace and Malagash, and took over certain established beds. It is expected that these beds would be turned over to private individuals who would lease them. Could the minister make a statement on this?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: The oyster developments around that area have been going on rather slowly. At Malagash arrangements are being made to construct a dike in an adjacent silt-free area. The department's object is to demonstrate the practicability of utilizing tide flats for the production of seed oysters, as is now done in many European countries and in parts of the United States. If successful, this method may prove to be the cheapest way of rearing small oysters. The great difficulty in the oyster industry is the rearing of small oysters.
What happens to the young oysters? Are they distributed throughout the district?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: They are placed in other areas.
There are some beds being developed for commercial purposes, and I should like to know what success has been achieved.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I have no information on that before me, but I can assure the hon. member that this matter is receiving very sympathetic attention.
This effort has been carried on for some time, and I understood one of the primary purposes was to establish beds for the commercial production of oysters in the Wallace harbour and Malagash area.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Very little interest has been shown by the local people in leases. We have not the details before us, but I know that in the Northumberland strait area the quantity of oysters has been increased by 100 barrels in 1949 over 1948. In 1948 the production was 3,500 barrels; in 1949 it was 3,600 barrels.
That does not indicate very great success. I understand that a good oyster bed will produce several hundred barrels per year per acre.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: But it takes a long time to develop it.
Only a few years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Oh, no, it takes from four to six years for oysters to grow to a merchantable size.

The life of an oyster is only four or five years. I understand that the effort is being made to bring some of these oyster beds back into production. There is practically an unlimited market for oysters from Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, because people all over Canada realize there is no better oyster to be found anywhere in the world. I am disappointed that the minister cannot give a more satisfactory report on these efforts that have been carried on for many years.

We have not the complete history before us, but I shall undertake to supply the hon. member with it. He is interested in this matter, and the success of the project depends upon the interest shown by the local people. We hope the interest shown by the hon. member will stimulate interest by others. This must be regarded as something in the nature of an experimental farm, and sometimes the results seem rather slow. They seem to be slow to me, and I can understand why they seem to be slow to the hon. member.

About ninety per cent of the clams that are shucked in Charlotte county, as well as most of the lobsters produced there, are shipped to the United States. In the past large clams have been shipped to the United States, but they have not been received favourably, and in many cases losses have been sustained by the shippers. The United States market demands a small clam. This may toe due to the fact that they are sold by the dozen at roadside stands and restaurants. The same thing applies to lobsters,
I understand it is hard for those who have little knowledge of the lobster industry to realize the difference between the price received for a chicken lobster and the price received for a select lobster. A chicken lobster will bring no more than 35 cents per pound on the market, whereas a select lobster is worth from 60 to 65 cents per pound. Whether we like it or not, we shall have to supply that market with the type of lobster they want and with the small clam they want.
When the large clam canneries are operating, the shuckers are able to sell the large clams to the canneries, but when they are closed there is quite a loss in that regard.
Supply-Fisheries
I ask the department to give serious consideration to changing the size limit so that these shucking plants may carry on. In my own constituency these plants employ quite a number of girls who make good money, and in my estimation they are responsible for the price of clams being higher today than at any time in the history of the country. I ask the department to consider seriously the .fact that we have to produce something that will sell, that we have to give the United States market the type of article they want over there.
Did the hon. member say that chicken lobsters were worth 65 cents a pound to the fisherman?
I quoted the prices paid by R. J. Conley Company at St. Andrews for live lobsters.
What does the fisherman receive at the boatside? He never gets more than 23 cents per pound.

I do not want to enter into an argument about price spreads. These lobsters are held in pounds for several months. They are purchased in Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and sometimes great losses result. R. J. Conley and Company ship lobsters to the United States 365 days in the year. Recently I was in their plant with the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and on that day they shipped 26,000 pounds of lobsters to the United States. More than ninety-six per cent of the lobsters they purchase are sold in the United States.

121.	To provide for transportation, dressing and
dyeing and other expenses incidental to receiving and disposing of fur seal skins accruing to Canada pursuant to provisional fur seal agreement between Canada and the United States by exchange of notes dated December 26, 1947, $500,000.
I should like to ask the minister for an explanation of this item of $500,000. This is what you spend but what do you get out of it? What profit is there to Canada?

The net profit to Canada oif the Pribilof seals last year was $682,000. Sixty-five per cent of our portion of the seals goes to the Fouke fur company in St. Louis for dressing, twenty-five per cent to C. W. Martin & Son, London, England, and ten per cent to Martin-Schnaufer Limited in Toronto. We have been checking with the firm in Toronto to see how they are getting along, and our latest information is that England is sending 400 of its seals to the Toronto factory for processing, indicating that there is a development taking place at Toronto.
You made a profit of three-quarters of a million dollars.
The net to Canada, including what we pay im customs duties, is $682,000.

I understand from what the minister says that you are sending a certain amount to the new plant in Toronto for processing. We know how the processing done in the United States compares with the processing of Martins of London, England; but how does the processing of the Canadian firm compare? In the last sale I noticed that skins processed in the United States brought the highest price. It is not a matter of how cheaply we can get the processing done. It is a question of the finished product, and one thing about which the department must be careful is to see that the finished article is kept up to the standard of those finished in the United States. If the seals are not properly processed and obtain a lower price than the same quality of skins processed in the United States, then it will be a bad thing for the industry in Canada.
As the minister has told the committee, there is enormous profit in the fur seal industry of the Pribylov islands. It is something that should be protected and looked after carefully. Going back to the year 1945, I made inquiries at that time and found that there was a profit of $136,000, and we were spending nearly $300,000. Today there is an enormous profit, and it can be greater still if, through co-operation between the governments of Canada and the United States, we decide to take off a greater number of skins. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I understand that for this year they 
decided to take off about twenty-five per cent more skins than last year. However, that will be verified from the results of what they do at the Pribilof islands.

Mr. Chairman, generally
speaking Canada has received more for skins processed in St. Louis than for those processed in England. For that reason the amount sent to England was considerably less than that sent to the United States. I think we would be pretty severely criticized, however, if we did not give the Toronto firm some skins to prove whether or not they can do the work in Canada. We do not know whether it will be successful because we have not yet had any finished skins from the Toronto plant. Apparently London is satisfied that their curing is equally good, because they have sent some of their own skins from England to be finished in the Toronto plant. I should like to at least give our own people a fair chance in order to ascertain whether they can or cannot do the work.
The prices of the various cured skins have varied from time to time, and in the last sale just a few days ago British cured skins brought a fairly good price.
I was not making any complaint about giving a percentage of the skins to the Toronto firm.
No.

What I say is if their processing is not equal to that of the United States, then by all means do not continue it, because our furs have a wonderful name and we might just as well keep it. The highest price realized at the St. Louis and Montreal sales was for a Canadian skin, the product of the Pribilof islands, which had been processed in St. Louis. I should like to know what is paid for processing in St. Louis, what is paid for processing of the same article to Martins of London, and also what is to be paid for processing at Toronto.

Does the hon. members mind if I give him that information tomorrow? We do not have it broken down in the way he 'wants it. I may say that the Martins company is a very old firm; also we felt that we did not want to risk putting all our eggs in the one basket, and for that reason our allotment was divided. Canada has a very high reputation for her furs, and we are not going to see her lose that reputation by accepting poorly cured seal skins, no matter where they come from.

minister give a comparative figure on the bounties that were paid in the county of Cumberland, Nova Scotia?

increase in this item, and I imagine that once again it is for the maritime provinces exclusively.

service for the maritimes with the member for Charlotte several times, and he has given me a lot of information about it. I have never understood it clearly. Will the minister explain exactly what service is provided?

government service which we took over from the Newfoundland government at the

time of confederation. They had bait storage depots and a refrigerator boat that went out to sea and brought in herring. These herring were put into the cold storages and later distributed as bait. The proposal was that the government would break even on it-that is, that they would do it on a cost basis. However, that was not the result before we took it over, and has not been the result since. Invariably there has been some loss in connection with it.

I am curious about this. Out on the Pacific coast, for instance, private concerns catch herring and put them in freezers. It is a regular part of their normal business. I do not believe it is a very sound principle-[DOT] it may be necessary and I am not criticizing the minister for having taken over this particular service and continuing it temporarily -for the federal fisheries department to be giving away bait.

I think the hon. member has to take into consideration the fact that there is a great deal of difference between the way fishing is handled in Newfoundland and the way it is handled in British Columbia. 126. To provide for the extension of educational work in co-operative producing and selling among fishermen, $80,000.

Will the minister explain
what this is? There are no details.
It is a grant to three universities for educational work among the fishermen.

I am renewing a request I made on a previous occasion when these estimates were up to see if some of this educational work in co-operative selling could not be done in Manitoba. The minister was going to consider it a year ago.

It is a little different in
Manitoba. In the inland provinces we do not administer the fisheries. The fathers of confederation were wise enough, I think, to put fisheries under the federal government; but when the natural resources were returned to certain of the provinces, the fisheries as well as other natural resources were transferred; therefore we cannot propose a unified plan for the whole of Canada and administer it without the co-operation of the provinces.

The money is voted for educational work in co-operative principles, and

that is why I was asking the minister if it was not possible to devise some way of doing some work in Manitoba.

If we do it for Manitoba we
will have to do it for practically every university across Canada. I do not know whether or not that would be good.

I am interested in this item. If any particular province is concerned with carrying on educational work in the development of co-operatives, not only for fishermen but fruit growers and others, would the dominion government-I presume the province makes a contribution-extend those services to other provinces that are willing to co-operate in the same way as the provinces in which these votes are spent?

I might say that in the province of Saskatchewan we have organized an educational extension department. At the present time it is taking up this matter of organizing the fishermen on the lakes into co-operatives to solve some of the problems they have there, just the same as the fishermen have problems in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and the other places. The province is carrying that work on. If the dominion are prepared to assist one province, I would think they would be prepared to assist other provinces that are prepared to go ahead and to do this type of educational work among the fishermen.

That is the job of the provincial government. They took over the natural resources. They want to administer them and we are allowing them to do so. If there is any way in which we can give them assistance, we shall naturally be prepared to do anything we can. But in doing what they are doing, they are only carrying out their responsibilities.

This item is for administration purposes, and I thought perhaps I might bring to the attention of the minister a question that I asked him some time ago about protection for the fishermen of Rustico, in my constituency. At the time I asked the question: What about the bombing range? I should now like to know if this bombing range has been definitely decided on; because a certain number of the fishermen, upon considering the matter, think that it will be detrimental to them if this bombing range is located where the officials were first talking about putting it. I had an answer from the minister, in a way, in which it was stated that they would look into the matter. Then when I put the question to the Minister of National Defence, he said that he had nothing further to add to what the Minister of Fisheries had said.

In justice to the fishermen I think that something definite should be given to them. There is no great necessity for taking this location for a bombing range when they already have a bombing range at Chatham in New Brunswick. If it is going to be outside the fourteen mile limit, that is a different question. But if it is just going to be outside the three mile limit, I am told-and I do not know whether it is correct-that it will destroy the fish in that area and that they will leave. I think the fishermen should have assurance as to whether it is going there, when it is going, or how it is they are to seek protection.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I can tell the hon. member for Queens that no firm decision has been made on the area for a bombing and gunnery range for Prince Edward Island.
No decision has been made?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: No decision has been made. Many negotiations have taken place and many meetings have been held with the fishermen of the area affected. I am sure that a site can be agreed upon which the majority of the fishermen will say is satisfactory. But it is purely in the preliminary stages.
The site is agreed upon?

speechtext:
No; it has not been
definitely agreed upon-"tentatively" probably would be a better word to use. But it is just in the preliminary stages. I do not think any more definite information can be given at the present time. It may never be used.

As I said a moment ago, it is not definitely needed when they have one a few miles farther away. Why should they subject the fishermen of that area to this hazard when they have one about thirty miles farther away? Thirty miles by air is not a great distance in these times. I would urge the Minister of Fisheries to take the matter up definitely with the Minister of National Defence. It will be up to the Minister of Fisheries to see that the protection needed out there is given. If it was in time of war and they wanted a second range, it would be a different matter. But they already have a range. For the sake of the distance of thirty miles, coming from Summerside, I do not think we should go after our fishermen so hard.
I have been in consultation with my colleague the Minister of National Defence, and I am quite prepared to assume the responsibility the hon. member has put on my shoulders.
